analysis.one_liner: Stops card companies from retroactively raising rates and piling fees on existing balances.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 312-112, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it before Congress ended, so it died without a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrote the rules of credit card accounts: card companies could no longer raise the interest rate on money you already owe just because you were late paying someone else, a practice called universal default, or charge interest using a two-cycle billing trick. It required 45 days notice before a rate increase, let you pay off your old balance at the old rate, stopped fees charged on balances consisting only of already-paid-off interest, limited over-the-limit fees, required statements 25 days before the due date, and barred credit cards for people under 18. The House passed it 312-112, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of credit cardholders, especially those who carry balances. The bill barred retroactive rate increases on money already borrowed (with narrow exceptions like a payment more than 30 days late), required a 45-day warning before any rate hike with the right to pay off the old balance at the old rate, banned interest charges on balances already paid in full, limited over-the-limit fees to once per billing cycle and let consumers opt out of them entirely, and required statements at least 25 days before the due date.

how_it_helps.text: Card companies could not raise the interest rate on an existing balance except when a public benchmark index moved, a promotional rate expired, or a payment was more than 30 days late — ending universal default triggered by unrelated late payments elsewhere.
Cardholders got 45 days written notice before a rate increase and could repay the existing balance at the old rate over at least five years.
The bill banned double-cycle billing, which charged interest on balances from earlier billing cycles that had already been paid off in full.

Consumers could opt out of over-the-limit transactions and their fees, over-limit fees were limited to once per billing cycle, and fees were barred when a credit hold pushed the balance over the limit.

Statements had to arrive at least 25 days before the due date, disclose how to obtain the payoff balance, and payments had to be allocated pro rata across balances with different rates so extra payments paid down the highest-rate debt.

Subprime 'fee harvester' cards that charged first-year fees above 25 percent of the credit line could no longer pay those fees out of the credit itself, and no credit card could be issued to anyone under 18.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, mostly large banks, which collected revenue from retroactive rate increases, universal default, double-cycle billing, and repeated over-limit fees. Critics warned issuers would offset the lost fee and interest revenue by charging all cardholders higher rates and new fees — a cost the bill did not directly address.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and large banks

drawbacks.text: The bill did not cap interest rates; cardholders could still see rates rise when a promotional rate expired, a benchmark index moved, or a payment was more than 30 days late.

Issuers argued the restrictions would cut revenue and be offset by higher rates and annual fees charged to all cardholders, including customers who paid in full — a general cost of restricting fee practices the bill left unaddressed.
The bill's protections applied to transactions starting one year after enactment, so cardholders would have waited up to a year for relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections addressed practices that hit people who already carried a balance and could not avoid them: a retroactive rate hike on money already borrowed, interest on debt already repaid, and repeated over-limit fees. The main real cost is that issuers would likely reprice their products, spreading some of the lost revenue across all cardholders through higher rates or fees, and the bill set no rate cap. On balance the bill traded a large, targeted benefit to indebted cardholders for a diffuse cost spread across the industry and its customers. Near-identical provisions became law in 2009 in the Credit CARD Act, which suggests the substance survived scrutiny when it finally got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 312-112, but the Senate Banking Committee took no action before the 110th Congress ended, so the bill died without ever getting a Senate vote.

narrative.text: Introduced in February 2008, the bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and reported out amended on September 16, 2008, by a 39-27 vote.
A Republican motion to recommit with instructions to add a trigger for enactment failed 198-219 on September 23, 2008, with 189 of 199 Republicans voting yes and 219 of 234 Democrats voting no.
The House passed the bill 312-112 on September 23, 2008, with 228 of 234 Democrats and 84 of 199 Republicans in favor.

The Senate received the bill on September 24, 2008, and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on October 2, 2008; the committee took no further action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers were better off because the bill died: they kept retroactive rate increases, universal default, double-cycle billing, and repeatable over-limit fees for the rest of the 110th Congress. Cardholders got nothing until near-identical rules passed as the Credit CARD Act the following year.

for.name: Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Credit Cardholders' Bill of Rights Act and steered it through the House.

for.name: House Committee on Financial Services
for.what_they_did: Discharged the subcommittee, held markup, and reported the bill as amended by a 39-27 vote on September 16, 2008.

against.name: Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill into committee on October 2, 2008 and took no further action on it before Congress ended.

against.name: Mike Castle
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a trigger for enactment; the motion failed 198-219.

against.name: Credit card issuers and the banking industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against restrictions on retroactive rate increases and fee practices.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was bipartisan: 228 of 234 Democrats and 84 of 199 Republicans voted yes, though the Republican motion to recommit split almost perfectly by party, 189-0 among Republicans to 9-219 among Democrats.

industries.note: The bill eliminated core profit drivers: retroactive rate increases on existing balances, universal default, double-cycle billing, and repeated over-limit fees. Issuers opposed it and would have had to reprice their products to recover the revenue.

Cards whose first-year fees exceeded 25 percent of the credit line could no longer charge those fees against the credit itself, threatening a business model built on upfront fees charged to people with weak credit.

Issuers could no longer report a newly opened card account until the consumer activated it, slightly reducing the flow of new-account data, though reporting applications and inquiries remained allowed.
